title: About Me
text:
I am a results-oriented Master’s student in Ireland specializing in Business Analytics and AI-driven business solutions. My work sits at the intersection of international trade and advanced analytics — translating complex data into strategic insights that inform real decisions.
My professional perspective is built upon a foundation in International Business and Trade, further enriched by practical experience in high-volume commercial environments across Mexico. During my time in customer-facing and operational roles, I developed an acute understanding of how supply chain dynamics, pricing fluctuations, and seasonal trends directly influence consumer behaviour. This firsthand observation of market variables served as the catalyst for my transition into advanced analytics.
I am currently refining my technical proficiency in Python, SQL, and Business Intelligence tools to translate complex datasets into actionable business intelligence. My goal is to combine my international business background with rigorous quantitative analysis to help organisations bridge the gap between global strategy and localised operational impact.

title: Global Development Trends: A Gapminder Analysis
text:
This project uses the Gapminder dataset — the same data that Hans Rosling used in his famous TED talks1 — to explore how the world has changed between 1952 and 2007. The dataset contains life expectancy, GDP per capita, and population for 142 countries across 12 five-year snapshots.






NoteQuestions this analysis answers




How has global life expectancy changed over time?
Is there still a strong link between wealth and longevity?
Which continents have gained the most?

title: Global Development Trends: A Gapminder Analysis
text:
This project uses the Gapminder dataset — the same data that Hans Rosling used in his famous TED talks1 — to explore how the world has changed between 1952 and 2007. The dataset contains life expectancy, GDP per capita, and population for 142 countries across 12 five-year snapshots.






NoteQuestions this analysis answers




How has global life expectancy changed over time?
Is there still a strong link between wealth and longevity?
Which continents have gained the most?

title: Global Development Trends: A Gapminder Analysis
section: The Relationship Between Wealth and Life Expectancy
text:
The Relationship Between Wealth and Life Expectancy


Show setup code
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = px.data.gapminder()
print(f"Dataset covers {df['country'].nunique()} countries across {df['year'].nunique()} years")
print(f"Years: {df['year'].min()} to {df['year'].max()}")


Dataset covers 142 countries across 12 years
Years: 1952 to 2007




Show the code
fig = px.scatter(
    df,
    x='gdpPercap',
    y='lifeExp',
    animation_frame='year',
    animation_group='country',
    size='pop',
    color='continent',
    hover_name='country',
    log_x=True,
    size_max=55,
    range_x=[100, 100000],
    range_y=[25, 90],
    title='Wealth vs Life Expectancy, 1952 to 2007',
    labels={
        'gdpPercap': 'GDP per Capita (USD, log scale)',
        'lifeExp': 'Life Expectancy (years)',
        'pop': 'Population'
    },
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=550)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Animated bubble chart: GDP per capita vs life expectancy over time. Press play to watch 55 years of progress.




This is the chart Hans Rosling made famous. The headline story is remarkable — across the period, every continent moved up and to the right. The world as a whole is healthier and wealthier than it was in 1952.

title: Global Development Trends: A Gapminder Analysis
text:
Life Expectancy Over Time


Show the code
continent_avg = df.groupby(['year', 'continent'])['lifeExp'].mean().reset_index()

fig = px.line(
    continent_avg,
    x='year',
    y='lifeExp',
    color='continent',
    markers=True,
    title='Average Life Expectancy by Continent',
    labels={'lifeExp': 'Life Expectancy (years)', 'year': 'Year'},
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set1,
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=450)
fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Continental average life expectancy over time




Africa’s trajectory is notably different — the curve flattens around the 1990s, reflecting the devastating impact of the HIV/AIDS epidemic on sub-Saharan countries. Asia shows the steepest gains of any continent over the period.

title: Global Development Trends: A Gapminder Analysis
text:
The Gains, Ranked


Show the code
first_year = df[df['year'] == 1952][['country', 'continent', 'lifeExp']].rename(columns={'lifeExp': 'lifeExp_1952'})
last_year = df[df['year'] == 2007][['country', 'lifeExp']].rename(columns={'lifeExp': 'lifeExp_2007'})

change = first_year.merge(last_year, on='country')
change['gain'] = change['lifeExp_2007'] - change['lifeExp_1952']
top_gains = change.nlargest(15, 'gain').sort_values('gain')

fig = px.bar(
    top_gains,
    x='gain',
    y='country',
    color='continent',
    orientation='h',
    title='Top 15 Countries by Life Expectancy Gain (1952 → 2007)',
    labels={'gain': 'Years gained', 'country': ''},
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Bold,
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=500)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Top 15 countries by absolute gain in life expectancy, 1952 to 2007




Oman leads the table — a country that transformed its healthcare infrastructure dramatically over this period. Several Asian countries feature heavily, reflecting the rapid development seen in that region.

title: Global Development Trends: A Gapminder Analysis
text:
A Snapshot: 2007


Show the code
df_2007 = df[df['year'] == 2007]

fig = px.scatter(
    df_2007,
    x='gdpPercap',
    y='lifeExp',
    size='pop',
    color='continent',
    hover_name='country',
    log_x=True,
    size_max=60,
    title='The World in 2007',
    labels={'gdpPercap': 'GDP per Capita (USD, log scale)', 'lifeExp': 'Life Expectancy (years)'},
    template='plotly_white',
    trendline='ols',
    trendline_scope='overall',
    trendline_color_override='gray'
)
fig.update_layout(height=500)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: GDP vs life expectancy in 2007, the most recent year in the dataset




The relationship is still clearly logarithmic — each additional unit of wealth buys less longevity than the last. A country at USD 1,000 per capita gains far more years from doubling to USD 2,000 than a country at USD 30,000 would from doubling to USD 60,000.

    total_pop=('pop', 'sum')

summary_wide = summary.pivot(index='continent', columns='year', values='avg_life_exp').round(1)
summary_wide[[1952, 1977, 2007]].style.background_gradient(cmap='RdYlGn', axis=None)

title: Reflection
section: What I Set Out to Do
text:
What I Set Out to Do
When I started, the instructions looked straightforward: spin up a Quarto site, write some pages, push it to GitHub Pages. Done. The reality of actually making each piece work — and work together — was more involved than I expected. In hindsight, that gap between “should be simple” and “actually works” is itself the lesson.

title: Reflection
text:
Skills I Actively Built

Git and version control
I have used Git before for personal projects, but this was the first time I tried to commit incrementally rather than batching a day’s work into one giant push. Writing descriptive commit messages as I worked turned out to be useful beyond the rubric — when I broke the navbar at one point, git log let me pinpoint exactly which change caused the issue and revert cleanly. That pattern is something I will carry into future work.


Quarto
I came in treating Quarto as “Markdown with extras” and left understanding it as a serious publishing system. The separation between content (.qmd files), configuration (_quarto.yml), and styling (styles.scss) mirrors good software architecture. Changing the site’s colour scheme in one file and seeing it propagate everywhere was satisfying in a way that taught me why that separation matters.


Python for reproducible analysis
Embedding executable {python} chunks in prose changed how I think about technical writing. Instead of producing a chart in a notebook and screenshotting it into a document, the chart is the document. If the underlying data changes, the chart updates. This is closer to how analysis should work in a professional setting, and it is a workflow I will keep using.


Sass and design systems
The SCSS section was where I learned the most unexpected lesson. I started by copying a Bootswatch theme and tweaking colours. Then I realised I was repeating the same hex code in four places and that Sass variables existed for exactly this reason. Refactoring into variables taught me that design, like code, benefits from DRY principles.

title: Reflection
section: Challenges I Had to Work Through
text:
Challenges I Had to Work Through






WarningThings that did not work the first time




GitHub Pages deployment: The site initially 404’d because I had forgotten the .nojekyll file. Jekyll was silently eating files whose names started with an underscore.
Quarto listing page: My project cards showed up empty at first because I had placed the individual project files in the wrong subdirectory relative to the contents field.
SCSS not applying: Variables in scss:rules instead of scss:defaults — order matters.
Plotly charts not rendering: Forgot that fig.show() is needed in Quarto {python} chunks the same way it is in scripts, not notebooks.



Each of these cost me 20–40 minutes. Individually they are annoying; collectively they are where the real learning happened. Debugging deployment is a skill, and you only build it by having deployments break.

title: Reflection
text:
What I Would Do Differently

Set up deployment first, before any content. I wrote half the site before my first successful deploy. If I had deployed an empty skeleton on day one, I would have caught the .nojekyll issue earlier and with much less code to bisect.
Commit more often. My early commits covered too many changes. When something broke, I had to untangle which change caused it. Smaller, atomic commits would have made rollback trivial.
Write the reflection as I went. I am writing this at the end, from memory. If I had kept running notes, the reflection would have more concrete detail and less post-hoc reconstruction.

title: Reflection
section: How This Connects to Where I Am Going
text:
How This Connects to Where I Am Going
The skills this project exercised — reproducible analysis, version control discipline, configuration-driven design, publishing to the web — are the same skills I expect to use in any data or software role. Whether I end up writing reports for a team, publishing research, or shipping a product, the workflow of code → commit → render → publish will show up in some form. Having now done the full loop end-to-end on something that is actually live on the internet makes it feel less abstract.
More specifically, I want to:

Extend one of the projects into a fuller machine-learning write-up with model evaluation.
Write a blog post using the same Quarto setup — the infrastructure is already here.
Contribute to an open-source Quarto extension to give something back to the tool that made this possible.

title: Reflection
text:
A Closing Thought






Note



The best thing about this project was that it forced me to use a lot of small skills together. Any one of them alone is trivial; stitching them into something that works is where the difficulty — and the learning — lives.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
The Palmer Penguins dataset is a widely used alternative to the classic Iris dataset. It contains physical measurements of 344 penguins from three species — Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo — collected at the Palmer Station, Antarctica1.
In this project I explore how the four key morphological features separate the three species and whether bill dimensions alone are enough to distinguish them.






NoteQuestions this analysis answers




How do the three species differ in body size?
Can bill length and depth alone separate the species?
Are there sex-based differences within species?

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Species Distribution


Show the code
counts = df.groupby(['species', 'island']).size().reset_index(name='count')

fig = px.bar(
    counts,
    x='species',
    y='count',
    color='island',
    barmode='group',
    title='Penguin Counts by Species and Island',
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2,
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=400, showlegend=True)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Number of penguins per species and island




Interesting observation: Gentoo penguins appear only on Biscoe island, and Chinstrap only on Dream island, while Adelie are spread across all three. Island is effectively a strong predictor on its own.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Bill Dimensions: The Star Feature


Show the code
fig = px.scatter(
    df,
    x='bill_length_mm',
    y='bill_depth_mm',
    color='species',
    symbol='sex',
    size='body_mass_g',
    hover_data=['island', 'flipper_length_mm'],
    title='Bill Length vs Bill Depth by Species',
    labels={
        'bill_length_mm': 'Bill Length (mm)',
        'bill_depth_mm': 'Bill Depth (mm)'
    },
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Bold,
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=500)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(line=dict(width=1, color='DarkSlateGrey')))
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Bill length versus bill depth coloured by species. Clear clustering is visible.




This is a classic example of Simpson’s paradox in disguise. If you ignore species, bill length and bill depth appear negatively correlated. But within each species, they are positively correlated. The three species form visually distinct clusters, and this single plot suggests bill measurements alone could power a reasonable classifier.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Body Mass Distribution


Show the code
fig = px.box(
    df,
    x='species',
    y='body_mass_g',
    color='sex',
    points='all',
    title='Body Mass by Species and Sex',
    labels={'body_mass_g': 'Body Mass (g)'},
    color_discrete_sequence=['#ed8936', '#2c5282'],
    template='plotly_white'
)
fig.update_layout(height=450)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Body mass distribution by species and sex




Gentoo penguins are substantially larger than the other two species. Within every species, males are consistently heavier than females — a clean example of sexual dimorphism.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Correlation Matrix


Show the code
numeric_cols = ['bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm', 'flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g']
corr = df[numeric_cols].corr().round(2)

fig = px.imshow(
    corr,
    text_auto=True,
    aspect='auto',
    color_continuous_scale='RdBu_r',
    zmin=-1, zmax=1,
    title='Feature Correlation Matrix'
)
fig.update_layout(height=450, width=550)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Pearson correlation between the four numerical features




Flipper length and body mass are tightly correlated (0.87). Bill depth shows the negative correlation with other size features that the species-level analysis revealed is actually paradoxical.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Key Takeaways






TipSummary




The three species are well-separated in bill-dimension space.
Gentoo is the largest species by a clear margin.
Island alone is a strong proxy for species — useful for quick classification.
Sexual dimorphism is present within every species.
